Amanda, it is Bruno. I am on the site and I have a crew waiting. Two questions, and I need the rule, not an opinion.
Go ahead. I will tell you what the rule says first, and what I recommend afterwards.
First one. Do we have to measure the area before we plant, or can that wait?
You have to measure first. The baseline must be established before any planting, and it must be done by the verification body.
Understood. Second one. The old trees at the edge. The crew says clearing them would save two days.
No. Existing forest must not be cleared, and the permit is explicit about it. That one is not a judgement call.
And the timing? The rain starts in six weeks and the certification people have not confirmed a date.
There the rule allows you to start. You may plant before the certificate arrives. But you should wait for the measurement, because without it the credits might not count.
So: measure first, do not touch the old trees, and after that it is my decision.
Exactly. And I will put those three lines in writing today, so that nobody has to remember this call in two years.

Amanda, it is Bruno, the project manager in the north. I am on the site now and I have two questions that the team keeps asking me, and I do not want to answer them wrongly. First, the old trees at the edge of the area. They are not many and they are not healthy, and the planting crew says it would be faster to clear them. I told them to wait for you. Second, the timing. The certification people have not confirmed a date, and the rain starts in six weeks. If we wait for the certificate, we lose the season, and if we plant now, I do not know whether the credits still count. I am not asking you to guess. I am asking you to tell me what the rule says, and what you recommend. Call me when you can.

Welcome back. In this part of the session I want to talk about the three words that decide whether a project produces credits or produces nothing. The first is baseline. The baseline is the level of emissions there would be without the project, and everything you claim is measured against it, so if the baseline is wrong, every number after it is wrong too. The second is additionality. Additionality is the proof that the reduction would not have happened anyway, and it is the hardest one, because you are proving something about a world that does not exist. The third is monitoring. A project must report, year after year, what it actually did, and a verification body has to check it. And here is the part that surprises lawyers. None of these three is mainly a scientific question. All three are questions of evidence, and evidence is your job.

Start with what the rule obliges, using must or have to. Then say what it forbids, with cannot or must not. Then say what it allows, with may or can. Then say what you recommend, with should. And finally, say what might happen if the recommendation is ignored.
